claim: Human intelligence relies on efficient processing by neurons in the brain.
source: It is generally assumed that human intelligence relies on efficient processing by neurons in our brain.
evidence: This is stated as a general assumption in the abstract.

claim: Grey matter thickness of temporal and frontal cortical areas correlates with IQ scores.
source: Although grey matter thickness and activity of temporal and frontal cortical areas correlate with IQ scores, no direct evidence exists that links structural and physiological properties of neurons to human intelligence.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, referencing prior research.

claim: High IQ scores associate with larger temporal cortical thickness.
source: Here, we find that high IQ scores and large temporal cortical thickness associate with larger, more complex dendrites of human pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: High IQ scores associate with larger, more complex dendrites of human pyramidal neurons.
source: Here, we find that high IQ scores and large temporal cortical thickness associate with larger, more complex dendrites of human pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Larger dendritic trees enable pyramidal neurons to track activity of synaptic inputs with higher temporal precision due to fast action potential kinetics.
source: We show in silico that larger dendritic trees enable pyramidal neurons to track activity of synaptic inputs with higher temporal precision, due to fast action potential kinetics.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling stated in the abstract.

claim: Human pyramidal neurons of individuals with higher IQ scores sustain fast action potential kinetics during repeated firing.
source: Indeed, we find that human pyramidal neurons of individuals with higher IQ scores sustain fast action potential kinetics during repeated firing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Human intelligence is associated with neuronal complexity, action potential kinetics and efficient information transfer from inputs to output within cortical neurons.
source: These findings provide the first evidence that human intelligence is associated with neuronal complexity, action potential kinetics and efficient information transfer from inputs to output within cortical neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Experimental research on the neurobiological basis of intelligence has largely ignored the neuronal level.
source: Thus far, experimental research on the neurobiological basis of intelligence has largely ignored the neuronal level and has not directly tested what role human neurons play in cognitive ability, mainly due to the inaccessibility of human neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature in the introduction.

claim: Research on intelligence has focused on finding genetic loci that explain variance in intelligence in large cohorts.
source: Instead, research has either been focused on finding genetic loci that can explain part of the variance in intelligence (Spearman's g) in large cohorts (Lam et al., 2017; Sniekers, 2017; Trampush et al., 2017; Coleman et al., 2018) or on identifying brain regions in whole brain imaging studies of which structure or function correlate with IQ scores (Karama et al., 2009; Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Narr et al., 2007; McDaniel, 2005; Deary et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Research on intelligence has focused on identifying brain regions whose structure or function correlate with IQ scores.
source: Instead, research has either been focused on finding genetic loci that can explain part of the variance in intelligence (Spearman's g) in large cohorts (Lam et al., 2017; Sniekers, 2017; Trampush et al., 2017; Coleman et al., 2018) or on identifying brain regions in whole brain imaging studies of which structure or function correlate with IQ scores (Karama et al., 2009; Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Narr et al., 2007; McDaniel, 2005; Deary et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Variability in brain volume and intelligence may share a common genetic origin.
source: Some studies have highlighted that variability in brain volume and intelligence may share a common genetic origin (Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Posthuma et al., 2002; Sniekers, 2017), and individual genes that were identified as associated with IQ scores might aid intelligence by facilitating neuron growth (Sniekers, 2017; Coleman et al., 2018) and directly influencing neuronal firing (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individual genes associated with IQ scores might aid intelligence by facilitating neuron growth.
source: Some studies have highlighted that variability in brain volume and intelligence may share a common genetic origin (Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Posthuma et al., 2002; Sniekers, 2017), and individual genes that were identified as associated with IQ scores might aid intelligence by facilitating neuron growth (Sniekers, 2017; Coleman et al., 2018) and directly influencing neuronal firing (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited research.

claim: Individual genes associated with IQ scores might aid intelligence by directly influencing neuronal firing.
source: Some studies have highlighted that variability in brain volume and intelligence may share a common genetic origin (Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Posthuma et al., 2002; Sniekers, 2017), and individual genes that were identified as associated with IQ scores might aid intelligence by facilitating neuron growth (Sniekers, 2017; Coleman et al., 2018) and directly influencing neuronal firing (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited research.

claim: Intelligence is a distributed function that depends on activity of multiple brain regions.
source: Intelligence is a distributed function that depends on activity of multiple brain regions (Deary et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cortical volume and function of specific areas correlate with general intelligence (g).
source: Structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging studies in hundreds of healthy subjects revealed that cortical volume and function of specific areas correlate with g (Karama et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2008; Narr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Areas in frontal and temporal cortices show correlations of grey matter thickness and functional activation with IQ scores.
source: In particular, areas located in the frontal and temporal cortices show multiple correlations of grey matter thickness and functional activation with IQ scores: individuals with high IQ show larger grey matter volume of, for instance, Brodmann areas 21 and 38 (Choi et al., 2008; Deary et al., 2010; Karama et al., 2009; Narr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals with high IQ show larger grey matter volume of Brodmann areas 21 and 38.
source: In particular, areas located in the frontal and temporal cortices show multiple correlations of grey matter thickness and functional activation with IQ scores: individuals with high IQ show larger grey matter volume of, for instance, Brodmann areas 21 and 38 (Choi et al., 2008; Deary et al., 2010; Karama et al., 2009; Narr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical grey matter consists for a substantial part of dendrites.
source: Cortical grey matter consists for a substantial part of dendrites (Chklovskii et al., 2002; Ikari and Hayashi, 1981), which receive and integrate synaptic information and strongly affect functional properties of neurons (Bekkers and Häusser, 2007; Eyal et al., 2014; Vetter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dendrites receive and integrate synaptic information and strongly affect functional properties of neurons.
source: Cortical grey matter consists for a substantial part of dendrites (Chklovskii et al., 2002; Ikari and Hayashi, 1981), which receive and integrate synaptic information and strongly affect functional properties of neurons (Bekkers and Häusser, 2007; Eyal et al., 2014; Vetter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher order association areas in temporal and frontal lobes in humans harbor pyramidal neurons of extraordinary dendritic size and complexity.
source: Especially higher order association areas in temporal and frontal lobes in humans harbor pyramidal neurons of extraordinary dendritic size and complexity (Elston, 2003; Mohan et al., 2015) that may constitute variation in cortical thickness, neuronal function, and ultimately IQ.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pyramidal neurons of extraordinary dendritic size and complexity may constitute variation in cortical thickness, neuronal function, and ultimately IQ.
source: Especially higher order association areas in temporal and frontal lobes in humans harbor pyramidal neurons of extraordinary dendritic size and complexity (Elston, 2003; Mohan et al., 2015) that may constitute variation in cortical thickness, neuronal function, and ultimately IQ.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited research and logical inference.

claim: Neurons and their connections form the principal building blocks for coding, processing, and information storage in the brain and give rise to cognition.
source: These neurons and their connections form the principal building blocks for coding, processing, and information storage in the brain and give rise to cognition (Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Even slight changes in efficiency of information transfer by neurons may translate into large differences in mental ability.
source: Given their vast number in the human neocortex, even the slightest change in efficiency of information transfer by neurons may translate into large differences in mental ability.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the large number of neurons.

claim: The study collected a multimodal data set from 46 human subjects containing single cell physiology (31 subjects, 129 neurons), neuronal morphology (25 subjects, 72 neurons), pre-surgical MRI scans and IQ test scores (35 subjects).
source: To investigate whether structural and functional properties of neurons of the human temporal cortex associate with general intelligence, we collected a unique multimodal data set from 46 human subjects containing single cell physiology (31 subjects, 129 neurons), neuronal morphology (25 subjects, 72 neurons), pre-surgical MRI scans and IQ test scores (35 subjects, Figure 1, data available at the Dryad Digital Repository: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.83dv5j7).
evidence: This describes the data collection for the study.

claim: Human cortical brain tissue was removed as part of surgical treatment for epilepsy or tumor.
source: Human cortical brain tissue was removed as a part of surgical treatment for epilepsy or tumor (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the source of tissue samples.

claim: The tissue almost exclusively originated from middle temporal gyrus, approximately 4 cm posterior to the temporal pole.
source: The tissue almost exclusively originated from middle temporal gyrus, approximately 4 cm posterior to the temporal pole (Figure 2b) as a block of ~1–1.5 cm in diameter and was removed to gain access to the disease focus in deeper lying structures such as hippocampus or amygdala.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of tissue samples.

claim: The resected neocortical tissue was not part of the epileptic focus or tumor and displayed no structural/functional abnormalities.
source: In all patients, the resected neocortical tissue was not part of the epileptic focus or tumor and displayed no structural/functional abnormalities in preoperative MRI investigation, electrophysiological whole-cell recordings or microscopic investigation of histochemically stained tissue (Mohan et al., 2015; Testa-Silva et al., 2014; Testa-Silva et al., 2010; Verhoog et al., 2016; Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the quality control of tissue samples, supported by citations.

claim: No correlations of cellular parameters or IQ scores with the subject's disease history and age were observed.
source: In line with the non-pathological status of tissue, we observed no correlations of cellular parameters or IQ scores with the subject's disease history and age (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Average cortical thickness in temporal lobe positively correlates with IQ scores from the same subjects (n subjects = 35).
source: (d) Average cortical thickness in temporal lobe (from area highlighted in red in c) positively correlates with IQ scores from the same subjects (n subjects = 35).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d with statistical correlation.

claim: Mean cortical thickness in temporal lobes positively correlated with IQ scores of the subjects.
source: In line with findings in healthy subjects (Choi et al., 2008; Deary et al., 2010; Hulshoff Pol et al., 2006; Narr et al., 2007;Karama et al., 2009) mean cortical thickness in temporal lobes positively correlated with IQ scores of the subjects (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2d and consistent with cited prior research.

claim: Cortical association areas in temporal lobes play a key role in high-level integrative neuronal processes.
source: Cortical association areas in temporal lobes play a key role in high-level integrative neuronal processes and its superficial layers harbor neurons of increased neuronal complexity (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston, 2003; Scholtens et al., 2014; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Superficial layers of cortical association areas in temporal lobes harbor neurons of increased neuronal complexity.
source: Cortical association areas in temporal lobes play a key role in high-level integrative neuronal processes and its superficial layers harbor neurons of increased neuronal complexity (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston, 2003; Scholtens et al., 2014; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In rodents, the neuropil of cortical association areas consists for over 30% of dendritic structures.
source: In rodents, the neuropil of cortical association areas consists for over 30% of dendritic structures (Ikari and Hayashi, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dendritic length positively correlated with mean temporal lobe cortical thickness (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.5, explained variance R2 = 0.25).
source: We found that dendritic length positively correlated with mean temporal lobe cortical thickness (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.5, explained variance R2 = 0.25), indicating that dendritic structure of individual neurons contributes to the overall cytoarchitecture of temporal cortex (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Dendritic structure of individual neurons contributes to the overall cytoarchitecture of temporal cortex.
source: We found that dendritic length positively correlated with mean temporal lobe cortical thickness (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.5, explained variance R2 = 0.25), indicating that dendritic structure of individual neurons contributes to the overall cytoarchitecture of temporal cortex (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: Cell bodies of pyramidal neurons with larger dendrites typically lie deeper, at larger distance from pia.
source: TDL is in part determined by the soma location within cortical layers: cell bodies of pyramidal neurons with larger dendrites typically lie deeper, at larger distance from pia (Mohan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no correlation between IQ score and relative cortical depth of pyramidal neurons.
source: There was no correlation between IQ score and relative cortical depth of pyramidal neurons indicating that we sampled neurons at similar depths across subjects (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding that rules out sampling bias.

claim: Individual's pyramidal neuron total dendritic length positively correlates with IQ scores (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.51, explained variance R2 = 0.26).
source: We found a strong positive correlation between individual's pyramidal neuron TDL and IQ scores (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.51, explained variance R2 = 0.26; Figure 3c) as well as between number of dendritic branch points and IQ scores (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.22; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Number of dendritic branch points positively correlates with IQ scores (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.22).
source: We found a strong positive correlation between individual's pyramidal neuron TDL and IQ scores (Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.51, explained variance R2 = 0.26; Figure 3c) as well as between number of dendritic branch points and IQ scores (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.22; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Larger and more complex pyramidal neurons in temporal association area may partly contribute to thicker cortex and link to higher intelligence.
source: Thus, larger and more complex pyramidal neurons in temporal association area may partly contribute to thicker cortex and link to higher intelligence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation findings.

claim: Dendritic morphology and ionic conductances act in concert to regulate neuronal excitability.
source: Dendrites not only receive most synapses in neurons, but dendritic morphology and ionic conductances act in concert to regulate neuronal excitability (Bekkers and Häusser, 2007; Eyal et al., 2014; Vetter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In model simulations, increasing the dendritic membrane surface area speeds up the onset phase of action potentials.
source: In model simulations where neurons are reduced to balls and sticks, increasing the dendritic membrane surface area, that is the dendritic impedance load, speeds up the onset phase of APs.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: The decrease in effective time constants of the neuron with increasing dendritic size and dendritic impedance load causes faster AP onset.
source: This is a consequence of the decrease in the effective time constants of the neuron with increasing dendritic size and dendritic impedance load (Eyal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an explanation based on cited research.

claim: Larger dendrites act as a larger sink for currents generated in the axon initial segment during AP onset and result in faster membrane potential changes.
source: Larger dendrites act as a larger sink for currents generated in the axon initial segment during AP onset and result in faster membrane potential changes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on biophysical principles.

claim: Human neocortical pyramidal neurons are three times larger than rodent pyramidal neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found previously that human neocortical pyramidal neurons, which are three times larger than rodent pyramidal neurons (Mohan et al., 2015), have faster AP onsets compared to rodent neurons and are able to track and encode fast synaptic inputs and sub-threshold changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human neocortical pyramidal neurons have faster AP onsets compared to rodent neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found previously that human neocortical pyramidal neurons, which are three times larger than rodent pyramidal neurons (Mohan et al., 2015), have faster AP onsets compared to rodent neurons and are able to track and encode fast synaptic inputs and sub-threshold changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human neocortical pyramidal neurons are able to track and encode fast synaptic inputs and sub-threshold changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision.
source: Furthermore, we found previously that human neocortical pyramidal neurons, which are three times larger than rodent pyramidal neurons (Mohan et al., 2015), have faster AP onsets compared to rodent neurons and are able to track and encode fast synaptic inputs and sub-threshold changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Total dendritic length of model neurons with realistic dendritic trees positively correlated with the steepness of AP onsets (r = 0.4, R2 = 0.16).
source: We found that TDL of model neurons with realistic dendritic trees positively correlated with the steepness of AP onsets (r = 0.4, R2 = 0.16; Figure 4a,b) and larger dendrites enabled neurons to generate faster APs.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: Larger dendrites enabled model neurons to generate faster APs.
source: We found that TDL of model neurons with realistic dendritic trees positively correlated with the steepness of AP onsets (r = 0.4, R2 = 0.16; Figure 4a,b) and larger dendrites enabled neurons to generate faster APs.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: The exact timing of action potential firing allows cortical neurons to pass on temporal information provided by synaptic inputs.
source: The exact timing of action potential firing allows cortical neurons to pass on temporal information provided by synaptic inputs (Köndgen et al., 2008; Ilin et al., 2013; Testa-Silva et al., 2014; Linaro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Single pyramidal neurons do not sustain high frequency firing and generally do not encode high frequency synaptic input content in rate coding.
source: Single pyramidal neurons do not sustain high frequency firing and generally do not encode high frequency synaptic input content in rate coding.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about pyramidal neurons.

claim: The precision in timing of AP initiation allows pyramidal neurons to encode incoming high frequency information in their output.
source: Instead, the precision in timing of AP initiation does allow these neurons to encode incoming high frequency information in their output.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about pyramidal neurons.

claim: Human neurons can encode sub-threshold membrane potential changes on a sub-millisecond timescale by timing of APs.
source: In contrast to rodent neurons, human neurons can encode sub-threshold membrane potential changes on a sub-millisecond timescale by timing of APs (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Synaptic input tracking capacity strongly relies on the rapidity of AP onset.
source: This synaptic input tracking capacity strongly relies on the rapidity of AP onset (Ilin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Faster APs allow neurons to respond to fast synaptic inputs, which will be missed if AP generation is too slow.
source: Faster APs allow neurons to respond to fast synaptic inputs, which will be missed if AP generation is too slow.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: Neurons with faster APs can translate higher frequencies of synaptic membrane potential fluctuations into AP timing and ultimately encode more information.
source: Thereby, neurons with faster APs can translate higher frequencies of synaptic membrane potential fluctuations into AP timing and ultimately encode more information.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: Neurons with larger dendritic compartments have faster AP onset rapidity according to theoretical work using 'ball-and-stick' neuron models.
source: The aforementioned theoretical work (Eyal et al., 2014) using 'ball-and-stick' neuron models showed that neurons with larger dendritic compartments not only have faster AP onset rapidity, but could also time AP generation to faster changes in membrane potentials, increasing the frequency tracking capabilities of input modulations, and augmenting the input frequency bandwidth of information encoding about three times.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical research.

claim: Neurons with larger dendritic compartments could time AP generation to faster changes in membrane potentials, increasing the frequency tracking capabilities of input modulations, and augmenting the input frequency bandwidth of information encoding about three times.
source: The aforementioned theoretical work (Eyal et al., 2014) using 'ball-and-stick' neuron models showed that neurons with larger dendritic compartments not only have faster AP onset rapidity, but could also time AP generation to faster changes in membrane potentials, increasing the frequency tracking capabilities of input modulations, and augmenting the input frequency bandwidth of information encoding about three times.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical research.

claim: Human neurons with larger TDL can reliably time their APs to faster membrane potential changes, with cut-off frequencies up to 400–500 Hz.
source: We find that human neurons with larger TDL can reliably time their APs to faster membrane potential changes, with cut-off frequencies up to 400–500 Hz, while smaller neurons had their cut-off frequencies already at 200 Hz (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: Smaller human neurons had their cut-off frequencies already at 200 Hz.
source: We find that human neurons with larger TDL can reliably time their APs to faster membrane potential changes, with cut-off frequencies up to 400–500 Hz, while smaller neurons had their cut-off frequencies already at 200 Hz (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the dendritic length and the cut-off frequency.
source: Furthermore, there was a significant positive correlation between the dendritic length and the cut-off frequency (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Larger neurons were able to better encode rapidly changing temporal information into timing of AP firing, compared to smaller neurons.
source: Finally, given the same input - composed of the sum of three sinusoids of increasing frequencies - larger neurons were able to better encode rapidly changing temporal information into timing of AP firing, compared to smaller neurons (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Differences in dendritic length of human neurons lead to faster APs and thereby to wider frequency bandwidths of encoding synaptic inputs into timing of AP output.
source: Thus, we find that differences in dendritic length of human neurons lead to faster APs and thereby to wider frequency bandwidths of encoding synaptic inputs into timing of AP output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: AP maximum rise speed depended on the firing history of the cell, with the first AP in the train having the highest AP rise speed and slowing down with increasing instantaneous firing frequency.
source: Maximum rise speed of APs depended on the firing history of the cell, with the first AP in the train having the highest AP rise speed and slowing down with increasing instantaneous firing frequency, the time interval between subsequent APs (Figure 5b–d).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The AP rise speed of the first AP was not different between high and low IQ groups.
source: Although the AP rise speed of the first AP was not different between high and low IQ groups (Figure 5c), the AP slowed down stronger in individuals with lower IQ scores compared to APs of individuals with higher IQ scores (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The AP slowed down stronger in individuals with lower IQ scores compared to APs of individuals with higher IQ scores.
source: Although the AP rise speed of the first AP was not different between high and low IQ groups (Figure 5c), the AP slowed down stronger in individuals with lower IQ scores compared to APs of individuals with higher IQ scores (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: At higher instantaneous firing frequencies (20–40 Hz), the AP rise speed was higher in individuals with IQ scores above 100 (AP rise speed high IQ = 338.4 ± 26.03 mV/ms; AP rise speed low IQ = 268.1 ± 12.20 mV/ms, t-test p=0.0113).
source: At higher instantaneous firing frequencies (20–40 Hz), the AP rise speed was higher in individuals with IQ scores above 100 (Figure 5c right; AP rise speed high IQ = 338.4 ± 26.03 mV/ms; AP rise speed low IQ = 268.1 ± 12.20 mV/ms, t-test p=0.0113).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: In neurons from individuals with lower IQ scores, AP rise speed at 20–40 Hz decreased to 74% of the initial AP rise speed.
source: Relative to first AP, rise speed at 20–40 Hz showed significant slowing in subjects with lower IQ scores and decreased to 74% of the initial AP rise speed.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In neurons from individuals with higher IQ scores, AP rise speed remained on average at 84% (high IQ = 0.84 ± 0.014; low IQ = 0.74 ± 0.024, t-test p value=0.037).
source: In contrast, in neurons from individuals with higher IQ scores, AP rise speed remained on average at 84% (Figure 5d right, high IQ = 0.84 ± 0.014; low IQ = 0.74 ± 0.024, t-test p value=0.037).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The AP rise speed of the first AP in the train positively correlated with IQ scores (r = 0.41, R2 = 0.17).
source: The AP rise speed of the first AP in the train positively correlated with IQ scores (r = 0.41, R2 = 0.17; Figure 5e), and this correlation was even stronger for AP rise speeds at instantaneous frequencies of 20–40 Hz (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.21; Figure 5f).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: AP rise speeds at instantaneous frequencies of 20–40 Hz positively correlated with IQ scores (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.21).
source: The AP rise speed of the first AP in the train positively correlated with IQ scores (r = 0.41, R2 = 0.17; Figure 5e), and this correlation was even stronger for AP rise speeds at instantaneous frequencies of 20–40 Hz (r = 0.46, R2 = 0.21; Figure 5f).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Relative AP values showed significant positive correlations with IQ (r = 0.37, R2 = 0.14).
source: Importantly, also relative AP values showed significant positive correlations with IQ, indicating that it is the relative slowing of APs at high frequencies that associates with intelligence (r = 0.37, R2 = 0.14; Figure 5g).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: It is the relative slowing of APs at high frequencies that associates with intelligence.
source: Importantly, also relative AP values showed significant positive correlations with IQ, indicating that it is the relative slowing of APs at high frequencies that associates with intelligence (r = 0.37, R2 = 0.14; Figure 5g).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: Larger neurons show less slowing of AP rise speed (higher relative AP speeds) at 20–40 Hz (r = 0.55, R2 = 0.30).
source: We find that larger neurons show less slowing of AP rise speed (higher relative AP speeds) at 20–40 Hz (r = 0.55, R2 = 0.30; Figure 5h).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Higher IQ scores are accompanied by faster APs during repeated AP firing, while lower IQ scores associate with increased AP fatigue during elevated neuronal activity.
source: These findings reveal that higher IQ scores are accompanied by faster APs during repeated AP firing, while lower IQ scores associate with increased AP fatigue during elevated neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons from individuals with higher IQ scores are better equipped to process synaptic signals at high rates and at faster time scales, which is necessary to encode large amounts of information accurately and efficiently.
source: Thus, neurons from individuals with higher IQ scores are better equipped to process synaptic signals at high rates and at faster time scales, which is necessary to encode large amounts of information accurately and efficiently.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Faster AP rise speed during neuronal activity and more complex, extended dendrites associate with higher intelligence.
source: Our findings provide a first insight into the possible cellular nature of human intelligence and explain individual variation in IQ scores based on neuronal properties: faster AP rise speed during neuronal activity and more complex, extended dendrites associate with higher intelligence.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: AP kinetics have profound consequences for information processing.
source: AP kinetics have profound consequences for information processing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In vivo, neurons are constantly bombarded by high frequency synaptic inputs.
source: In vivo, neurons are constantly bombarded by high frequency synaptic inputs and the capacity of neurons to keep track and phase-lock to these inputs determines how much of this synaptic information can be passed on to other neurons (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The capacity of neurons to keep track and phase-lock to high frequency synaptic inputs determines how much of this synaptic information can be passed on to other neurons.
source: In vivo, neurons are constantly bombarded by high frequency synaptic inputs and the capacity of neurons to keep track and phase-lock to these inputs determines how much of this synaptic information can be passed on to other neurons (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The brain operates at a millisecond time-scale and even sub-millisecond details of spike trains contain behaviorally relevant information that can steer behavioral responses.
source: The brain operates at a millisecond time-scale and even sub-millisecond details of spike trains contain behaviorally relevant information that can steer behavioral responses (Nemenman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: One of the most robust and replicable findings in behavioral psychology is the association of intelligence scores with measures of cognitive information-processing speed.
source: Indeed, one of the most robust and replicable findings in behavioral psychology is the association of intelligence scores with measures of cognitive information-processing speed (Barrett et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reaction times (RT) in simple RT tasks provide a better prediction of IQ than other speed-of-processing tests, with a regression coefficient of 0.447.
source: Specifically, reaction times (RT) in simple RT tasks provide a better prediction of IQ than other speed-of-processing tests, with a regression coefficient of 0.447 (Vernon, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High positive correlations between RT and other speed-of-processing tests suggest the existence of a common mental speed factor.
source: In addition, high positive correlations between RT and other speed-of-processing tests suggest the existence of a common mental speed factor (Vernon, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Classic findings on the association between reaction time and intelligence were confirmed in a large longitudinal population-based study counting more than 2000 participants.
source: Recently, these classic findings were confirmed in a large longitudinal population-based study counting more than 2000 participants (Der and Deary, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Especially strong correlations between RT and general intelligence were reported for a slightly more complex 4-choice task.
source: Especially strong correlations between RT and general intelligence were reported for a slightly more complex 4-choice (Der and Deary, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results provide a biological cellular explanation for mental speed factors: in conditions of increased mental activity or more demanding cognitive task, neurons of individuals with higher IQ are able to sustain fast action potentials and can transfer more information content from synaptic input to AP output.
source: Our results provide a biological cellular explanation for such mental speed factors: in conditions of increased mental activity or more demanding cognitive task, neurons of individuals with higher IQ are able to sustain fast action potentials and can transfer more information content from synaptic input to AP output.

claim: Pyramidal cells are integrators and accumulators of synaptic information.
source: Pyramidal cells are integrators and accumulators of synaptic information.

claim: Larger dendrites can physically contain more synaptic contacts and integrate more information.
source: Larger dendrites can physically contain more synaptic contacts and integrate more information.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on structural properties.

claim: Human pyramidal neuron dendrites receive twice as many synapses as in rodents.
source: Indeed, human pyramidal neuron dendrites receive twice as many synapses as in rodents (DeFelipe et al., 2002) and cortico-cortical whole-brain connectivity positively correlates with the size of dendrites in these cells (Scholtens et al., 2014; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cortico-cortical whole-brain connectivity positively correlates with the size of dendrites in pyramidal cells.
source: Indeed, human pyramidal neuron dendrites receive twice as many synapses as in rodents (DeFelipe et al., 2002) and cortico-cortical whole-brain connectivity positively correlates with the size of dendrites in these cells (Scholtens et al., 2014; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study found almost 2-fold larger dendritic arbor size (mean TDL = 14.67 ± 4 mm) and number of dendritic branches (64.03 ± 17.7) compared to reports that use post-mortem tissue.
source: In this and a previous study (Mohan et al., 2015), we find almost 2-fold larger dendritic arbor size (mean TDL = 14.67 ± 4 mm) and number of dendritic branches (64.03 ± 17.7) compared to reports that use post-mortem tissue (Jacobs et al., 2001; Bianchi et al., 2013; Elston et al., 2001).

claim: The differences in dendritic size could be explained by advantages of biocytin filled neurons in surgical resections compared to Golgi stainings in human post-mortem tissue.
source: The differences could be explained by a number of advantages of biocytin filled neurons in surgical resections compared to traditionally used Golgi stainings in human post-mortem tissue.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The cortical slices in the study are thicker (350 μm compared to 120–250 μm) and contain neurons with almost completely intact apical and basal dendrites.
source: The cortical slices in our study are thicker (350 μm compared to 120–250 μm) and contain neurons with almost completely intact apical and basal dendrites, while other studies use only basal dendrites for quantification (Jacobs et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison with prior studies.

claim: Other studies use only basal dendrites for quantification.
source: The cortical slices in our study are thicker (350 μm compared to 120–250 μm) and contain neurons with almost completely intact apical and basal dendrites, while other studies use only basal dendrites for quantification (Jacobs et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison with prior studies.

claim: Only a small number of neurons are filled in a slice, which allows to unambiguously quantify all dendrites from individual cells.
source: Furthermore, only a small number of neurons are filled in a slice, which allows to unambiguously quantify all dendrites from individual cells.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of the study's approach.

claim: The tissue comes from a living donor compared to post-mortem tissue collection, and thus does not suffer from post-mortem delays and only still living functional cells are filled.
source: Importantly, the tissue comes from a living donor compared to post-mortem tissue collection, and thus does not suffer from post-mortem delays (de Ruiter, 1983) and only still living functional cells are filled.

claim: Post-mortem studies make it possible to make comparative analysis of several cortical areas.

claim: A gradient in complexity of pyramidal cells in cortical superficial layers accompanies the increasing integration capacity of cortical areas.
source: A gradient in complexity of pyramidal cells in cortical superficial layers accompanies the increasing integration capacity of cortical areas, indicating that larger dendrites are required for higher-order cortical processing (Elston et al., 2001; Jacobs et al., 2001; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larger dendrites are required for higher-order cortical processing.
source: A gradient in complexity of pyramidal cells in cortical superficial layers accompanies the increasing integration capacity of cortical areas, indicating that larger dendrites are required for higher-order cortical processing (Elston et al., 2001; Jacobs et al., 2001; van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neuronal complexity gradient also exists from individual to individual and could explain differences in mental ability.
source: Our results align well with these findings, suggesting that the neuronal complexity gradient also exists from individual to individual and could explain differences in mental ability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings in the context of prior research.

claim: Within human cortex, association areas contain neurons with larger and more complex dendrites than primary sensory areas.
source: Within human cortex, association areas contain neurons with larger and more complex dendrites than primary sensory areas, while neuronal cell body density is lower in cortical association areas compared to primary sensory areas (Elston, 2003; DeFelipe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal cell body density is lower in cortical association areas compared to primary sensory areas.
source: Within human cortex, association areas contain neurons with larger and more complex dendrites than primary sensory areas, while neuronal cell body density is lower in cortical association areas compared to primary sensory areas (Elston, 2003; DeFelipe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larger neurons are not as tightly packed together within cortical space as smaller cells.
source: Larger neurons are not as tightly packed together within cortical space as smaller cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on structural properties.

claim: A study by Genç et al., 2018 used multi-shell diffusion tensor imaging to estimate parieto-frontal cortical dendritic density and found that higher IQ scores correlated with lower values of dendritic density.
source: A recent study by Genç et al., 2018 used multi-shell diffusion tensor imaging to estimate parieto-frontal cortical dendritic density and found that higher IQ scores correlated with lower values of dendritic density (Genç et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Lower dendritic density in parieto-frontal cortical areas in individuals with higher IQ scores may indicate that these areas have less densely packed neurons, and may suggest that these neurons are larger.
source: This may indicate that parieto-frontal cortical areas in individuals with higher IQ scores have less densely packed neurons, and may suggest that these neurons are larger.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior research findings.

claim: Taking the results of Genç et al., 2018 and the current study together may suggest that the neuronal circuitry associated with higher intelligence is organized in a sparse and efficient manner, where larger and more complex pyramidal cells occupy larger cortical volume.
source: Taking the results of Genç et al., 2018 and our study together may suggest that the neuronal circuitry associated with higher intelligence is organized in a sparse and efficient manner, where larger and more complex pyramidal cells occupy larger cortical volume.
evidence: This is a speculative synthesis of the current study's findings with prior research.

claim: Larger dendrites have an impact on excitability of cells.
source: Larger dendrites have an impact on excitability of cells (Bekkers and Häusser, 2007; Vetter et al., 2001) and determine the shape and rapidity of APs (Eyal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larger dendrites determine the shape and rapidity of APs.

claim: Increasing the size of dendritic compartments in silico lead to acceleration of AP onset and increased encoding capability of neurons.

source: Both in models and in slice recordings, changes of AP initiation dynamics were shown to fundamentally modify encoding of fast changing signals and the speed of communication between ensembles of cortical neurons (Eyal et al., 2014; Ilin et al., 2013).

claim: Neurons with fast AP onsets can encode high frequencies and respond quickly to subtle input changes.
source: Neurons with fast AP onsets can encode high frequencies and respond quickly to subtle input changes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The ability to encode high frequencies can be impaired and response speed is decreased when AP onsets are slowed down by experimental manipulations.
source: This ability can be impaired and response speed is decreased when AP onsets are slowed down by experimental manipulations (Ilin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results demonstrate that AP speed depends on dendritic length and influences information transfer.
source: Our results not only demonstrate that AP speed depends on dendritic length and influences information transfer, but also show that both dendritic length and AP speed in human neurons correlate with intelligence.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Both dendritic length and AP speed in human neurons correlate with intelligence.
source: Our results not only demonstrate that AP speed depends on dendritic length and influences information transfer, but also show that both dendritic length and AP speed in human neurons correlate with intelligence.

claim: Individuals with larger dendrites are better equipped to transfer synaptic information at higher frequencies.
source: Thus, individuals with larger dendrites are better equipped to transfer synaptic information at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Dendritic morphology and different parameters of AP waveform are parameters that show pronounced differences between humans and other species.
source: Remarkably, dendritic morphology and different parameters of AP waveform are also parameters that we have previously identified as showing pronounced differences between humans and other species (Mohan et al., 2015; Testa-Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human pyramidal cells in layers 2 and 3 have 3-fold larger and more complex dendrites than in macaque or mouse.
source: Human pyramidal cells in layers 2 and 3 have 3-fold larger and more complex dendrites than in macaque or mouse (Mohan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human APs have lower firing threshold and faster AP onset kinetics both in single APs and during repeated firing.
source: Moreover, human APs have lower firing threshold and faster AP onset kinetics both in single APs and during repeated firing (Testa-Silva et al., 2014).

claim: Differences across species emphasize specific adaptations of human pyramidal cells in association areas for cognitive functions.
source: These differences across species may suggest evolutionary pressure on both dendritic structure and AP waveform and emphasize specific adaptations of human pyramidal cells in association areas for cognitive functions.

claim: In all patients, the resected neocortical tissue was not part of epileptic focus or tumor and displayed no structural or functional abnormalities in preoperative MRI, electrophysiological recordings or microscopic investigation of stained tissue.

evidence: This addresses potential concerns about the representativeness of the findings.

claim: None of the parameters correlated with age at epilepsy onset, seizure frequency, age or disease duration.
source: Secondly, none of the parameters correlated with age at epilepsy onset, seizure frequency, age or disease duration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This addresses potential concerns about the representativeness of the findings.

claim: IQ, dendritic length or AP rise speed were not different across different patient groups.
source: Thirdly, IQ, dendritic length or AP rise speed were not different across different patient groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This addresses potential concerns about the representativeness of the findings.

claim: The cortical thickness correlation with general intelligence observed in the study was also reported in hundreds of healthy subjects.
source: Finally, the cortical thickness correlation with general intelligence we observe in our study was also reported in hundreds of healthy subjects.
evidence: This addresses potential concerns about the representativeness of the findings by comparing with prior research.

claim: The findings are not likely to be influenced by disease background of the subjects.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that our findings are not likely to be influenced by disease background of the subjects.

source: In this study, intelligence was measured using WAIS IQ score, that combines results of 11 individual subtests of cognitive functioning into a single full-scale IQ score (Wechsler, 2008; Taylor and Heaton, 2001).
evidence: This describes the methodology for measuring intelligence.

claim: Using WAIS IQ score inevitably simplifies and reduces a multi-dimensional human trait to a single number.
source: This inevitably simplifies and reduces a multi-dimensional human trait to a single number.

claim: IQ tests have proven their validity and relevance.
source: Although none of the intelligence tests can capture all aspects of human intelligence, IQ tests have proven their validity and relevance.

claim: The results of different cognitive subtests are highly correlated and generate a strong general factor – general intelligence or Spearman's g.
source: The results of different cognitive subtests are highly correlated and generate a strong general factor – general intelligence or Spearman's g (Spearman, 1904).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

source: Spearman's g, calculated based on subtests of WAIS and expressed in total full-scale IQ score, strongly correlates with highly relevant life outcomes, including education, occupation, and income (Strenze, 2007; Foverskov et al., 2017).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Full scale IQ score provides a relevant and meaningful estimation of general intelligence that lies at the core of cognitive differences between individuals.
source: Thus, despite its shortcomings, full scale IQ score provides a relevant and meaningful estimation of general intelligence that lies at the core of cognitive differences between individuals.

claim: At the level of individual neurons, dendritic size and ability to maintain fast responses link to general mental ability.
source: In conclusion, our results provide first evidence that already at the level of individual neurons, such parameters as dendritic size and ability to maintain fast responses link to general mental ability.

claim: Very small changes in dendritic size and AP speed parameters, multiplied by an astronomical number of cortical neurons, may lead to large differences in encoding capabilities and information transfer in cortical networks.
source: Multiplied by an astronomical number of cortical neurons in our brain, very small changes in these parameters may lead to large differences in encoding capabilities and information transfer in cortical networks and result in a speed advantage in mental processing and, finally, in faster reaction times and higher cognitive ability.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Small changes in neuronal parameters may result in a speed advantage in mental processing and, finally, in faster reaction times and higher cognitive ability.
